title: The Cessation of Hostilities: A Winter to Rearm
content:
At noon on 1 January 1995, a cessation of hostilities agreement brokered by former United States President Jimmy Carter took effect across Bosnia-Herzegovina. The war was thirty-three months old. The ceasefire was intended to last four months, creating space for diplomatic efforts to produce a broader settlement. It was the most significant pause in fighting since the conflict began in April 1992, and both sides understood its true purpose from the outset: not peace, but preparation.

The Carter ceasefire emerged from the wreckage of previous diplomatic failures. The Vance-Owen plan, the Owen-Stoltenberg plan, and the Contact Group plan had each collapsed under the weight of incompatible territorial demands. The Bihac crisis of late 1994 had demonstrated the continued intensity of the fighting and the inadequacy of UNPROFOR's mandate. Carter's personal diplomacy with Radovan Karadzic in Pale produced an agreement where professional negotiators had failed, though the terms were loose and enforcement mechanisms virtually nonexistent. The agreement required a complete cessation of offensive military operations, the separation of forces along existing front lines, and the facilitation of humanitarian aid deliveries.

Compliance was partial from the first day. Sniping continued in Sarajevo. Artillery exchanges occurred along front lines in central Bosnia and the Posavina corridor. Neither side withdrew heavy weapons as the agreement nominally required. UNPROFOR monitors documented persistent violations but lacked the authority or capability to enforce the terms. The ceasefire held in the sense that large-scale offensive operations ceased, but the daily violence of the war continued at a reduced tempo.

What both sides did with the respite was far more consequential than what they refrained from doing. The Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina used the winter months to reorganize its corps structure, integrate equipment that had been acquired through various channels despite the international arms embargo, and conduct training. The ARBiH that would fight in the spring and summer of 1995 was a markedly more capable force than the one that had entered the ceasefire. Corps-level command and control improved. Logistics systems were rationalized. The Washington Agreement of March 1994, which had ended the Bosniak-Croat war and created the Federation, was now bearing military fruit as coordination with Croatian forces deepened.

The VRS used the same period to concentrate forces for operations that had been under planning for months. The Drina Corps, responsible for eastern Bosnia, quietly repositioned assets in preparation for what would become the assaults on the eastern enclaves. As established in both the ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T) and the Mladic Trial Judgment (IT-09-92-T), the Bosnian Serb military and political leadership used the ceasefire period to advance planning for operations against Srebrenica and Zepa. The concentration of forces near the enclaves during the ceasefire months was not incidental but deliberate.

The diplomatic track that the ceasefire was supposed to enable produced nothing of substance. The fundamental territorial dispute remained unresolved. The Bosnian Serb leadership, controlling approximately seventy percent of Bosnia's territory with roughly a third of its population, rejected any settlement that would require significant territorial concession. The Bosnian government, backed by the Contact Group's proposed fifty-one to forty-nine percent territorial split, refused to accept the permanence of ethnic cleansing.

The ceasefire expired on 1 May 1995 without renewal. Within days, the war resumed at an intensity that would exceed anything seen in the previous two years. The four-month pause had not brought the belligerents closer to agreement. It had given them time to sharpen their weapons for the final and most violent phase of the conflict.
